goldens.comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/index.ts:3 — The default appStore export now exposes promises instead of module objects, breaking every consumer that reads an app synchronously without a versioned compatibility boundary.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that packages/app-store/index.ts changed from static imports (import * as applecalendar from './applecalendar') to dynamic imports (applecalendar: import('./applecalendar')). This means appStore properties are now Promises instead of module objects. While the diff shows many call sites were updated to use 'await appStore[...]', the finding correctly identifies this is a breaking change. However, looking at the diff, the consumers shown ARE being updated to await the promises. The concern about 'versioned compatibility boundary' is valid but the diff shows the migration is being done. The issue is that forEach with async callbacks in vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts won't properly await the promises, which is a real bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/_utils/getCalendar.ts:9 — The exported getCalendar API changed from Calendar-or-null to Promise<Calendar-or-null>, so callers outside this repository will silently receive a truthy Promise and fail on Calendar methods.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows getCalendar's signature changed from synchronous (returning Calendar | null) to async (returning Promise<Calendar | null>). This is a breaking API change for external consumers who would receive a Promise object instead of the Calendar, causing their code to fail when calling Calendar methods. However, this is not strictly a 'bug' in the diff itself - the internal callers shown in the diff are properly updated to use await. The issue is about external API compatibility/breaking change, which is an important architectural concern but not a defect in the implementation shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts:125 — Async forEach is not awaited, so dynamic-import or deletion failures escape the surrounding try/catch and rescheduling can report success before cleanup finishes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that on line 125, the callback passed to forEach is changed to `async (bookingRef) => {...}` and inside it `await getCalendar(...)` is called. However, forEach does not await async callbacks - it ignores the returned promises. This means: 1) The try/catch block on line 123 won't catch any errors from the async operations since they run detached, 2) The function can complete/return before the calendar deletions finish, 3) Any failures in getCalendar or deleteEvent will be unhandled promise rejections. This is a real bug where async operations in forEach are not properly awaited.

adjudication_records.issue_text: packages/app-store/index.ts:3 — Constructing every dynamic-import promise at module initialization eagerly loads all app packages, so consumers still pay the full startup and memory cost instead of loading only the selected app.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misunderstands how dynamic imports work. In the new code, `import('./applecalendar')` returns a Promise that is created at module initialization, but the actual module loading (fetching, parsing, executing the module code) only happens when the Promise is awaited. The promises themselves are lightweight objects. The diff shows that consumers now use `await appStore[appName]` to resolve these promises on-demand, meaning the actual app code is only loaded when that specific app is accessed. This is the standard pattern for lazy loading with dynamic imports - the startup cost is NOT the same as eager static imports.
